question: What proportion of adults having hip fracture surgery receive intravenous tranexamic acid before the start of surgery?
why: NICE widened TXA to all adults whose surgery breaches the skin (NG24, 2026). One hip fracture audit in the corpus [1725] reached 85% with protocol and teaching; nobody has audited against the 2026 wording.

standard.source: NICE NG24 rec 1.3.1 and 1.3.3 (2015, updated February 2026)
standard.wording: 1.3.1 Offer tranexamic acid to adults having surgery in an operating theatre if: there is any risk of bleeding and the procedure will breach the skin or mucous membranes. [2026] ... 1.3.3 When using tranexamic acid for adults having surgery, administer it just before the start of surgery. Typically give 1 g by slow intravenous injection. [2026]

pass: TXA given IV between induction and knife-to-skin, recorded on the anaesthetic chart; or a specific contraindication documented.
population: Adults (≥60) having surgery for hip fracture. Exclude patients managed without surgery.
sample: 40 consecutive operated hip fracture patients over the last 6 weeks.
data_source: NHFD extract for case list; anaesthetic chart or anaesthetic e-record for TXA dose and time; theatre system for knife-to-skin time.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a default 'Tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction' line to the hip fracture anaesthetic e-record or pre-printed chart, with an 'omitted because' box.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive operated hip fractures, same template.
close_loop: Present at the joint anaesthetic and trauma governance meeting. If it works, make the default line permanent and add TXA to the monthly hip fracture dashboard.
evidence: [1725] hip fracture TXA: 70% → 85% (protocol update and teaching; p=0.23)
[2572] HPB: TXA prompt on WHO time-out did not increase pre-operative dosing (checklist prompt alone fails)
[1743] trust-wide e-record monitoring: 78.7% → 86.3% overall, T&O 98.2% (electronic tracking)
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the anaesthetic e-record

question: What proportion of red cell transfusions for non-bleeding hip fracture patients are given as a single unit followed by reassessment?
why: Back-to-back two-unit transfusions are common on trauma wards. The corpus has threshold audits [1254][1294] but single-unit practice was only measured once (54.2%) with no loop.

standard.source: NICE NG24 rec 1.6.1 and 1.6.2 (2015, updated February 2026)
standard.wording: 1.6.1 Consider single‑unit red blood cell transfusions for adults (or equivalent volumes calculated based on body weight for children or adults with low body weight) who do not have active bleeding. [2015] 1.6.2 After each single‑unit red blood cell transfusion (or equivalent volumes calculated based on body weight for children or adults with low body weight), clinically reassess and check haemoglobin levels, and give further transfusions if needed. [2015]

pass: One unit prescribed per episode, and a documented Hb check or clinical review before any further unit.
population: Transfusion episodes in adults admitted with hip fracture. Exclude major haemorrhage and active bleeding documented at the time.
sample: 40 consecutive transfusion episodes in hip fracture patients over the last 3–4 months.
data_source: Blood bank issue log (Trust transfusion lab) for episodes; EPMA or transfusion chart for units prescribed; lab system for Hb between units; notes for review.

reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive episodes, same template.
close_loop: Present with the hospital transfusion practitioner at the transfusion committee. If it works, extend the 1-unit default to all T&O wards.

[2515] general surgery: back-to-back units 20.5% → 4.5% (teaching and posters)
[1294] T&O: inappropriate transfusions 73.5% → 45.5% (teaching and induction booklet)

question: What proportion of older adults admitted with a pelvic fragility fracture receive pharmacological VTE prophylaxis for one month?
why: Pelvic and acetabular fragility fractures are often managed non-operatively outside the hip pathway. NICE gives them the same one-month prophylaxis as hip fractures. No audit in corpus; the NHFD adds pelvic fractures from 2026.

standard.wording: Offer VTE prophylaxis for a month to people with fragility fractures of the pelvis, hip or proximal femur if the risk of VTE outweighs the risk of bleeding. Choose either: LMWH, starting 6 to12 hours after surgery or fondaparinux sodium, starting 6 hours after surgery, providing there is low risk of bleeding. [2018]

pass: LMWH or fondaparinux prescribed in hospital and on discharge to cover 28 days or more from admission; or a documented reason (bleeding risk, already anticoagulated).
population: Adults ≥60 admitted with a low-energy pelvic ring or acetabular fracture. Exclude high-energy trauma and patients on therapeutic anticoagulation.
sample: 30 consecutive admissions over the last 6–9 months.
data_source: Admissions or coding list (ICD-10 S32.1–S32.8) or NHFD pelvic dataset; EPMA for inpatient doses; discharge prescription (TTO) for days supplied.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

reaudit: Wk 13–14 (or when 30 new cases accrue): next consecutive admissions, same template.

[1691] arthroplasty: 90% → 98% (discharge pack and nurse check)
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from EPMA and TTO

question: What proportion of hip fracture patients whose surgery is delayed beyond the day after admission receive pre-operative pharmacological VTE prophylaxis?
why: About four in ten patients miss surgery by the day after admission (NHFD KPI 2 national 57%). Delayed patients lie immobile without cover. No audit in corpus measures pre-operative prophylaxis in this group.

standard.wording: Consider pre‑operative VTE prophylaxis for people with fragility fractures of the pelvis, hip or proximal femur if surgery is delayed beyond the day after admission . Give the last dose no less than 12 hours before surgery for LMWH or 24 hours before

pass: At least one pre-operative dose of LMWH (or fondaparinux) given after the day of admission, with the last dose ≥12 h (LMWH) before surgery; or a documented reason not to.
population: Adults ≥60 with hip fracture operated later than the day after admission. Exclude patients on therapeutic anticoagulation.
sample: 40 consecutive delayed patients from the last 3 months of NHFD data.
data_source: NHFD extract (admission and surgery times) to find delayed cases; EPMA administration record for LMWH doses and times.

question: What proportion of hip fracture patients who had delirium in hospital have the delirium diagnosis written in the discharge summary to the GP?
why: About a third of hip fracture patients fail the post-op 4AT (NHFD KPI 5 national 68% pass). Delirium raises later dementia risk, but GPs are rarely told. 4AT screening is heavily audited; the hand-over is not.

standard.wording: Ensure that the diagnosis of delirium is documented both in the person's record or notes, and in their primary care health record. [2010]

pass: The discharge summary sent to the GP names delirium (or acute confusional state) as a diagnosis or complication of this admission.
population: Adults with hip fracture who had delirium in hospital (post-op 4AT ≥4 or delirium diagnosed in notes). Exclude deaths in hospital.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible discharges over the last 3–4 months.
data_source: NHFD extract (post-op 4AT score) to identify cases; notes for diagnosis; electronic discharge summary.

question: What proportion of hip fracture patients with delirium still present at discharge have a plan for cognitive follow-up?

population: Adults with hip fracture whose last 4AT before discharge was ≥4, or whose notes say delirium unresolved. Exclude known dementia already under a memory service.
sample: 30 consecutive eligible discharges over the last 6 months.
data_source: NHFD extract and orthogeriatric notes for last 4AT; discharge summary; memory service referral system.

question: What proportion of hip fracture inpatients staying longer than 7 days have their malnutrition screen repeated every week?
why: Weight loss after hip fracture is common and admission MUST is usually done. Weekly repeats are not. Only 2 nutrition audits in hip fracture in the corpus; one elderly-care audit found 48% weekly MUST [1848].

standard.wording: All hospital inpatients on admission and all outpatients at their first clinic appointment should be screened. Screening should be repeated weekly for inpatients and when there is clinical concern for outpatients.

pass: A MUST (with a recorded weight) on admission and at least every 7 days until discharge.
population: Adults with hip fracture with length of stay >7 days. Exclude end-of-life care.
sample: 40 consecutive discharges over the last 2 months.
data_source: NHFD extract for length of stay; nursing e-record for MUST dates and weights.

question: What proportion of DXA scans done after a fragility fracture in women aged 60 and over or men aged 70 and over include a vertebral fracture assessment?
why: Most vertebral fractures are silent and change treatment choice. NICE NG259 (July 2026) now advises VFA with DXA in these age groups. No audit in corpus.

standard.wording: Consider doing a VFA when doing a DXA scan for: men aged 70 and over women aged 60 and over.

pass: VFA done and reported with the DXA; or a documented reason not to (spinal imaging in past 3 months, scoliosis, body mass limit).
population: Women ≥60 and men ≥70 having DXA via the fracture liaison service after a fragility fracture.
sample: 40 consecutive FLS DXA scans over the last 1–2 months.
data_source: DXA service reports; DXA request forms; FLS database.

question: What proportion of adults aged 50 and over with a newly reported vertebral fracture on CT are identified by the fracture liaison service?
why: Radiology reporting of vertebral fractures is audited [1569][1683] but not whether the patient reaches the FLS. Onward referral was recommended in 2.6% of reports nationally [1569].

standard.source: Royal Osteoporosis Society Clinical Standards for FLS, standard 1.1 (September 2025)
standard.wording: 1.1. The FLS identifies people aged 50 years or older presenting with a new fragility fracture. This includes: • Newly identified vertebral fracture. (a prevalent vertebral fragility fracture which has not been previously documented)

pass: Patient appears on the FLS database or has an FLS referral within 12 weeks of the CT report.
population: Adults ≥50 with a CT (chest, abdomen, pelvis or spine) report newly describing a vertebral fracture, wedge or compression deformity. Exclude trauma CTs, known myeloma or metastases, and patients already on the FLS database.
sample: 40 consecutive reports over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: RIS free-text search ('vertebral fracture', 'wedge', 'compression', 'loss of height'); FLS database.
